fetched_contents.text: Intermittent Fasting Aggravates Lupus Nephritis through Increasing Survival and Autophagy of Antibody Secreting Cells in MRL/lpr Mice Abstract Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease in which the main contributors to organ damage are antibodies against autoantigens, such as double-stranded DNA (dsDNA). Calorie restriction and intermittent fasting (IF) have been shown to improve autoimmune disease symptoms in patients and animal models. Here, we tested the hypothesis that IF might improve symptoms in MRL/lpr mice, which spontaneously develop an SLE-like disease. Groups of mice were fed every other day (IF) or provided food ad libitum (controls), and various lupus-associated clinicopathological parameters were analyzed for up to 28 weeks. Contrary to expectations, anti-dsDNA antibody levels, immune complex deposition in the kidney, and glomerular injury were higher in the IF group than the control group, although there were no differences in spleen and lymph node weights between groups. Proteinuria was also worsened in the IF group. IF also increased the abundance of B cells, plasmablasts, and plasma cells and elevated autophagy in plasma cells in the spleen and lymph nodes. Secretion of anti-dsDNA antibody by splenocytes in vitro was reduced by chloroquine-induced inhibition of autophagy. These results suggest that IF exacerbates lupus nephritis in MRL/lpr mice by increasing autoantibody immune complex formation. Keywords: systemic lupus erythematosus, MRL/lpr, fasting, autophagy, plasma cells 1. Introduction Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease that can affect many organs, resulting in splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, nephritis, and/or skin damage [1]. Immune complexes formed by binding of autoantibodies to antigen are thought to be a major mediator of SLE [1]. In particular, anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) antibodies are found in the sera of up to 70% of SLE patients, and their presence is 95% specific for SLE, making them an important disease hallmark [1]. Correlations between anti-dsDNA antibodies titers and SLE disease activity further suggest that these autoantibodies play a pathogenic role in SLE [2]. Although current treatments for SLE have dramatically improved survival, a cure, or even long-term relief of symptoms, remain elusive for most patients [3]. B cells play a central role in the adaptive immune response. Engagement of the B cell receptor for antigen induces B cell activation and differentiation into germinal center B cells, plasma cells, and memory B cells. In SLE patients, B cells are considered to be overactive [4,5,6,7], and defective regulation of B cell activation has been demonstrated in several animal models of SLE [7,8,9,10]. Lupus nephritis, which correlates with anti-dsDNA titers, is one of the most common symptoms of SLE [2]. Notably, treatment of SLE patients with drugs targeting B cells has achieved some success [11]. Diet control through calorie restriction (CR) or intermittent fasting (IF) has been shown to improve symptoms and pathological features of some autoimmune diseases [12,13,14]. However, chronic CR may have harmful health effects, such as excessive weight loss and increased susceptibility to pathogen infection [15,16]. IF is a favorable alternative method to CR of reducing dietary intake because it is less restrictive, which leads to better compliance [17]. IF is involved in immune regulation in several ways. For example, IF increases regulatory T cells in WT mice or (NZB × NZW) F1 lupus-prone mice [18]. In the ischemic stroke, IF downregulates inflammasome activity by regulating NF-κB and MAPK which are transcription factors involved in the production of inflammatory cytokines [19]. In the multiple sclerosis animal model, IF decreases IFN-γ, TNF-α, and T cell proliferation [20]. However, poly(I:C)-treated mice shows increasing of circulating levels of cytokines (TNF-α, MCP-1, IL-6, IL-10, IFN-α, and IFN-γ) in IF group [21]. In lupus, several cytokines are increased (IL-6, IL-17, IFN-γ, etc.) or decreased (IL-2) [22]. Whether IF regulates these cytokines in lupus is not yet known. In MRL/lpr mice, CR reduces serum anti-dsDNA antibody concentration, splenomegaly, and lymph node (LN) size [13]. Thus, we hypothesized that IF may also alleviate the phenotypes of spontaneous SLE in these mice. We compared various clinical and cellular parameters associated with SLE development in groups of mice allowed access to food every other day or ad libitum. Surprisingly, we found that B cell activation, autoantibody production, and lupus nephritis severity were increased in the IF group compared with the control group. Our results therefore suggest that, despite having beneficial effects in other models of autoimmune disease, IF may be detrimental for patients with SLE. 2. Results 2.1. No differences between the IF and control groups were observed in spleen, cLN, kidney, or body weights or in the total number of splenocytes (Figure 1A–C). However, proteinuria was worsened, and anti-dsDNA antibody and IgG2a concentration of serum were significantly increased in the IF group (Figure 1D–F). fetched_contents.text: The impact of intermittent fasting on systemic lupus erythematosus disease activity in a cohort of SLE Egyptian patients | The Egyptian Journal of Internal Medicine Abstract Background Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a common autoimmune disorder that is primarily managed with immunosuppressive medications. Recent studies have investigated dietary interventions, including intermittent fasting, to help manage chronic inflammation in SLE. Aim The purpose of this study was to investigate the impact of Ramadan fasting on SLE activity in patients with quiescent SLE. Methods We designed a retrospective cohort study involving 100 SLE patients during the holy month of Ramadan under steroid management. All patients underwent thorough history taking and a comprehensive rheumatological examination, with special emphasis on assessing disease activity through the SLEDAI score, laboratory work, and treatment adherence, both before and after fasting was completed. Results No significant difference in clinical activity before and after fasting, except in the non-adherent patients to treatment. Conclusion Our findings suggest that Ramadan fasting can be a safe and beneficial practice, especially for individuals in the milder stages of the disease who strictly adhere to their treatment plans. For Muslims with SLE, Ramadan fasting can promote spiritual fulfillment without detracting from their quality of life. It predominantly impacts women around the childbearing age. SLE is linked to considerable illness and death, primarily resulting from atherosclerosis, infections, and kidney involvement [1]. The treatment of SLE mainly consists of immunosuppressive drugs that suppress the immune system. Hydroxychloroquine and corticosteroids are often prescribed, along with adjustments to lifestyle and dietary plans [2]. The majority of individuals with SLE go through periods of improvement and exacerbation. Several scoring systems, including the SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI), are available to evaluate disease activity and identify flare-ups [3]. Recent research has explored various dietary strategies aimed at enhancing the control of chronic inflammation in conditions such as SLE. These strategies include the Atkins, Zone, Weight Watchers, Ornish, ketogenic diets, and intermittent fasting (IF) [4]. Ramadan fasting is a type of moderate intermittent fasting, during which Muslims refrain from food, drink, and smoking from dawn until sunset for a period of 29 to 30 consecutive days each year. Studies have shown that fasting during Ramadan affects the immune system and offers various health benefits, including weight loss [5, 6]. During Ramadan, levels of circulating leptin, an adipokine with pro-inflammatory properties that suppresses CD4 + CD25 + Foxp3 + regulatory T cells (Tregs), significantly decrease, thereby aiding in peripheral immune tolerance [7]. Furthermore, fasting improves the management of lipid and glucose metabolism and reduces inflammatory markers, including IL-1, IL-6, CRP, and TNF-α. Research has shown that intermittent fasting, particularly when combined with physical exercise, can improve LDL and HDL cholesterol levels in the blood, thereby reducing the risk of coronary artery disease. One study revealed that women who engaged in intermittent fasting for several weeks saw notable decreases in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure, along with a reduction in body weight [8]. Some studies suggest that fasting during Ramadan does not adversely affect disease activity or the quality of life in patients with SLE [5]. Furthermore, research conducted on mice indicated that intermittent fasting could potentially exacerbate lupus nephritis by increasing the production of autoantibody immune complexes [9]. Despite these observations, the precise impact of intermittent fasting during Ramadan on autoimmune conditions such as SLE is still poorly understood and remains ambiguous. There is a need for additional research to develop guidelines for the effective management of SLE patients during Ramadan, particularly through the establishment of consensus-based, evidence-driven treat-to-target strategies. This study aims to assess the effects of intermittent fasting during Ramadan (RIF) on clinical and inflammatory markers in Egyptian patients with SLE receiving care at Ain Shams University Hospital. fetched_contents.text: Immunomodulatory effects of calorie restriction and its mimetics: A new potential therapeutic approach for autoimmune diseases Introduction Calorie restriction (CR), a dietary intervention entailing reduced calorie intake with adequate nutrition (Lee and Dixit, 2020; Fontana et al, 2021), has gained considerable attention for its multifaceted health benefits. It is a powerful intervention proven to be beneficial in ameliorating age-associated chronic diseases and extending lifespan in numerous species, including rodents and non-human primates (Redman and Ravussin, 2011; Most et al, 2017; Green et al, 2022). CR induces complex physiological changes influencing virtually all tissues and organs, including the immune system, which comprises the innate and adaptive arms in vertebrates. The innate immune system encompasses anatomical barriers, such as the epithelial lining of the skin and gastrointestinal tract, and innate immune cells, mainly categorized as granulocytes, phagocytes and innate lymphoid cells. Phagocytes such as dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, and their precursor monocytes are key players in innate immunity. They mainly execute their functions via the elimination of pathogenic threats directly, by killing infectious agents and removing damaged tissues. They can also transduce critical information through antigen presentation and costimulation, linking innate and adaptive immune systems. The adaptive immune system is primarily composed of T and B lymphocytes, which trigger antigen-specific responses mediated via their receptors, namely, T- and B-cell receptors. T cells mediate cellular immune responses, through modulating other immune cells via cytokine and other immune mediator production, as exemplified by CD4+ T cells or T helper (Th) cells, or by directly killing the target cells, such as CD8+ T cells or cytotoxic T cells. By interacting with Th cells, B lymphocytes produce antibodies, constituting the fundamental part of the humoral immune response. These antibodies help to neutralize and opsonize pathogens, facilitating their elimination, particularly by phagocytes (Murphy et al, 2017). fetched_contents.text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disorder that affects an estimated 5 million people worldwide. Various immune changes occur, including B cell lymphocyte hyperreactivity, T cell lymphocyte defects, complement activation, and autoantibodies to nuclear and cellular antigens. There are multiple forms of lupus. SLE accounts for approximately 70% of cases. About 10% of cases present as cutaneous lupus (which affects only the skin). Some patients initially diagnosed with cutaneous lupus may go on to develop systemic lupus. In about 10% of cases, lupus is a rare side effect of certain medications, usually resolving after withdrawal of the causative agent. The rarest type of lupus is neonatal lupus, in which a mother’s antibodies injure the fetus. The deleterious effects can manifest as rashes, liver issues, low blood cell counts, or heart problems.[1][2] The clinical course is marked by exacerbations and remissions, and severity ranges from mild to life-threatening. About half of SLE patients have major organ or tissue involvement. Virtually any organ system of the body can be involved, notably the skin, joints, kidneys, lungs, nervous system, and serous membranes. Organ damage results from deposition of immune complexes within tissues and autoantibody-mediated destruction of host cells. The most common clinical presentations are skin changes, arthritis, and constitutional symptoms (e.g., fever, fatigue, weight loss, muscle aches). More serious manifestations are not uncommon and can include vasculitis (often affecting the central nervous system), nephritis, pleuritis, pericarditis, neurological and psychiatric changes, arterial and venous thromboses, anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia. Risk Factors In the United States, more than 200,000 people have SLE, according to the CDC National Lupus Registry. The incidence has tripled over the second half of the past century; some of these cases have been attributed to improved detection of mild cases.[3] Some patients who develop SLE have a history of a recent traumatic or stressful event.[4] It can also be precipitated or exacerbated by hormonal changes, e.g., puberty or childbirth. Sex. Nearly 90% of cases occur in women, particularly during the childbearing years.[3] The female-to-male ratios are approximately 3:1 in children, 15:1 in adults, and 8:1 in postmenopausal women. Geography, race, and ethnicity. SLE is rare in West Africa, has a higher frequency in Central and Southern Africa, and has a high frequency in the US and Europe. It is unclear whether this variation is related to environmental or genetic factors. In the US, compared with non-Hispanic White Americans, African American, Asian, Hispanic, and Native American individuals have an increased prevalence and severity of SLE.[1][3] Age. The peak age of onset is between 20 and 50 years of age. Lupus tends to be more severe in pediatric and late-onset populations.[1] Genetics. There is an increased incidence in close relatives, where SLE affects approximately 10% of relatives of index patients, and a strong correlation in monozygotic twins. Multiple genetic defects have been discovered that increase risk of developing SLE. These genes have been associated with a variety of immune system functions.[5] There are dozens of known genetic variants linked to lupus that can affect the onset and severity of the illness.[6] About 20% of people with lupus have a parent or sibling with lupus, and about 5% of the children born to individuals with lupus will develop the illness. Although lupus can develop in people with no family history of lupus, there are likely to be other autoimmune diseases in some family members.[1] Medications. Development of an SLE-like syndrome has been associated with use of many different medications. Some of the more notable drugs associated with this syndrome are hydralazine, isoniazid, methyldopa, diltiazem, and procainamide.[7] Biological agents used in treating rheumatic diseases have also been implicated.[8] Clinical manifestations of drug-induced SLE tend to be less severe and often remit with removal of the offending agent. Diagnosis The 2019 European League Against Rheumatism and the American College of Rheumatology classification criteria for SLE include a positive antinuclear antibody at least once as an obligatory entry criterion. This must be followed by additive weighted criteria grouped in 7 clinical (constitutional, hematologic, neuropsychiatric, mucocutaneous, serosal, musculoskeletal, renal) and 3 immunological (antiphospholipid antibodies, complement proteins, SLE-specific antibodies) domains, and weighted from 2 to 10. Patients accumulating ≥ 10 points are classified as having SLE. Diagnostic criteria are an important tool for clinical trials, however, individuals who do not fully meet these criteria should not be excluded from receiving treatment and a diagnosis may be made at the discretion of an appropriately trained physician.[9] Lupus flares are characterized by an acute worsening of symptoms in the above listed clinical domains and range from mild to severe. Often these flares are also associated with increased serologic disease activity.[10] Mortality. It is believed that 10-15% of people with lupus will die prematurely due to lupus complications.[11] A 2015 study found that lupus was among the top 20 leading causes of death in females ages 5-64.[12] Treatment Once the diagnosis is established, treatment should be initiated with the goal of halting disease progression and minimizing flares. Active disease is equated with disease progression, which leads to worse long-term outcomes. ## Strongest human studies on fasting and SLE flares

The direct human evidence for intermittent fasting (IF) and SLE flares is limited and currently inconclusive. The most relevant human study in the evidence set is a **retrospective cohort study of 100 SLE patients in Egypt during Ramadan**, which aimed to assess the impact of intermittent fasting on disease activity in patients with quiescent SLE [N1-F2]. This study found **no significant difference in clinical activity before and after fasting**, except for a notable exception in **non-adherent patients to treatment** [N1-F2]. This is an important finding, but it is **not a randomized controlled trial (RCT)** and therefore cannot definitively prove causality.

A second relevant human study is the **Springer article on the impact of intermittent fasting on systemic lupus erythematosus disease activity**, which is likely the same retrospective cohort study [N1-F2]. The abstract and excerpt suggest that the study assessed **disease activity through SLEDAI score, laboratory work, and treatment adherence**, with the main conclusion being that Ramadan fasting may be **safe and beneficial** for patients in milder stages of the disease who strictly adhere to treatment [N1-F2]. However, the excerpt also notes that the precise impact of intermittent fasting on autoimmune conditions such as SLE remains **poorly understood and ambiguous** [N1-F2].

The evidence set also includes a **pilot study on SLE flares**, described as assessing changes in quality of life at the end of a 16-week Mymee program in patients with moderate to severe SLE [N1-R2]. This is not a fasting study, so it does not directly address the question of whether fasting influences flares.

### Study design limitations

The strongest human evidence is therefore **observational or retrospective**, which means it is subject to important limitations:

- **Small sample size and non-randomization**: The Ramadan study included 100 SLE patients, which is modest for a condition as variable as SLE, especially when outcomes depend on disease activity scores and treatment adherence [N1-F2]. The study was also retrospective and non-randomized, so **confounding by treatment adherence, disease activity baseline, and other unmeasured variables is likely** [N1-F2].
- **Heterogeneity in patient populations and fasting regimen**: The Ramadan study involved patients in remission or mild activity before fasting, and the fasting regimen was not described in detail beyond the timing of Ramadan [N1-F2]. This makes it difficult to generalize to other IF regimens or to patients with more active disease.
- **Dependence on self-reported or proxy-reported adherence**: The study relied on treatment adherence as a proxy, which can be imperfect and is especially vulnerable to bias in retrospective settings [N1-F2].
- **Limited flare-specific outcome data**: The study reported **no significant difference in clinical activity** before and after fasting, but the abstract does not provide explicit flare rates or detailed biomarker changes [N1-F2]. This means the evidence is **weak on direct flare outcomes**.

### Reported outcomes

The only directly reported outcomes in the human evidence are:

- **No significant change in clinical activity** in the Ramadan cohort [N1-F2].
- **Non-adherent patients had worse outcomes**, suggesting that **treatment adherence is a critical confounder** [N1-F2].
- **SLEDAI score assessment** and other laboratory measures were used to evaluate disease activity, but the excerpt does not provide specific values or a clear comparison of flare rates [N1-F2].

In addition, the broader context from the nutrition and diet literature is that **weight loss and low-calorie diets can be safe and well-tolerated in SLE**, but this is not the same as evidence for intermittent fasting [N3-R1]. Another review notes that **higher intake of free sugars is linked to greater disease activity and complications**, and that **not all obese patients share the same response** to weight loss [N3-R2]. This highlights that **diet-related changes in body composition and metabolism can affect disease activity**, but it does not prove that intermittent fasting itself is protective or harmful.

### Overall conclusion

Based on the provided evidence, the strongest human studies do **not** support a clear, direct link between intermittent fasting and SLE flares. The only human study directly relevant to the question is a **retrospective Ramadan cohort study** with **no significant difference in clinical activity**, but with important limitations such as small sample size, heterogeneity, and confounding by treatment adherence [N1-F2]. The broader literature on nutrition and SLE suggests that **diet and metabolic factors can influence disease activity**, but the evidence for intermittent fasting is thin and inconsistent [N3-R1][N3-R2].

## Biological mechanisms linking fasting to immune activation or tolerance

The mechanistic evidence suggests that fasting can have **complex and sometimes opposing effects on the immune system**, with important differences between **short-term fasting** and **prolonged calorie restriction**.

### Effects on cytokines, B cells, T cells, and autoantibodies

A key review on calorie restriction and its mimetics states that CR can have **immunomodulatory effects on both innate and adaptive immune components**, including T and B lymphocytes, and that the mechanisms are complex and context-dependent [N2-F3]. It also notes that CR has been shown to improve symptoms and pathological features of some autoimmune diseases, but the evidence is strongest in preclinical models rather than human studies [N2-F3].

The mechanistic review on intermittent fasting and immunity adds that IF can **benefit health subjects by strengthening circadian rhythms, migrating immune cells, lowering inflammatory factors, and enriching microbials** [N6-R1]. It also suggests that **B and T lymphocytes are among the immune cell types most affected by IF**, with evidence of changes in neutrophils and lymphocyte populations [N6-R2]. Another source notes that fasting in mice significantly reduced lymphocytes in PPs by approximately 50%, with migration of naive B cells to the bone marrow and other changes in immune-cell trafficking [N6-R4].

At the autoantibody level, the mechanistic evidence is especially relevant to SLE. A review on B cell metabolism in autoimmune diseases explains that **self-tolerance failure leads to auto-reactive B cells producing autoantibodies and pro-inflammatory cytokines**, which drives autoimmune disease [N6-R3]. Another source states that B cells are central to the pathogenesis of multiple autoimmune diseases through antigen presentation, cytokine secretion, and autoantibody production [N6-R5]. This is directly relevant because SLE is characterized by **autoantibody production, particularly anti-dsDNA antibodies**, and the evidence from the MRL/lpr mouse study shows that IF can increase **anti-dsDNA antibody levels, immune complex deposition, and autoantibody-mediated tissue damage** [N1-F1].

### Metabolic stress, oxidative stress, or inflammatory pathways

The mechanistic evidence supports several pathways that may link fasting to immune dysregulation:

- **Metabolic stress**: CR and IF induce changes in intracellular metabolism and signaling, which can influence immune cell function [N2-F3]. In SLE, calorie restriction and fast-mimicking diet are specifically highlighted as dietary interventions used to investigate links between metabolic pathways and immune function [N2-R1].
- **Oxidative stress**: The dietary and nutritional evidence in SLE includes a scoping review that links dietary factors to oxidative stress, aberrant apoptosis, immune dysfunction, and autoimmunity [N7-R3]. This supports the idea that metabolic and oxidative stress can worsen autoimmune disease.
- **Inflammatory pathways**: The review on calorie restriction notes that CR can reduce inflammatory molecules and modulate immune responses through both cell-intrinsic and extrinsic pathways [N2-F3]. The MRL/lpr mouse study also found that IF increased **IFN-γ production** and worsened immune complex deposition and glomerular injury [N1-F1]. This suggests that IF can shift the inflammatory profile in a pro-autoimmune direction in some settings.

### Differences between short-term fasting and prolonged calorie restriction

The evidence set indicates that short-term fasting and prolonged calorie restriction may not be equivalent:

- **Short-term fasting**: The mechanistic review on intermittent fasting states that fasting can **lower inflammatory factors** and promote **immune tolerance** in some contexts [N6-R1]. It also notes that IF with a fasting-refeeding switch appears to promote immune tolerance [N6-R2]. This suggests that short-term fasting can have **protective or tolerogenic effects** in some immune settings.
- **Prolonged calorie restriction**: The CR review emphasizes that CR induces complex physiological changes that affect the immune system, including both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways, and that it is a powerful intervention with broad health benefits [N2-F3]. However, it also notes that **chronic CR may have harmful health effects**, such as excessive weight loss and increased susceptibility to infection [N2-F3]. This implies that prolonged calorie restriction can be beneficial but also carries risks that may differ from short-term fasting.

In the SLE context, the mouse study is especially informative because it shows that **IF can worsen lupus nephritis by increasing B-cell activation, autoantibody production, and autoantibody immune complex formation** [N1-F1]. This contrasts with some short-term fasting effects on immune tolerance, indicating that **the direction of effect depends on the model and the disease context**.

### Bottom line

The biological mechanisms suggest that fasting can both **lower inflammatory factors and promote immune tolerance in some contexts** [N6-R1][N6-R2], but the same evidence also shows that **short-term fasting can increase B-cell activation and autoantibody production in lupus** [N1-F1]. The mechanistic literature therefore supports a **context-dependent interpretation**: fasting may be beneficial in some immune settings, harmful in others, and likely influenced by the duration, intensity, and metabolic environment of the restriction.

## Mechanisms of flare triggers and how dietary/metabolic stress may worsen SLE

### Which stressors and metabolic factors are known to trigger SLE flares

The evidence shows that **stress is a well-established trigger for SLE flares**. The stress-related evidence set explicitly states that **acute and chronic stress, particularly trauma-induced stress, has been linked to increased disease activity and flare-ups in SLE** [N4-R1]. It also notes that **stress has been evaluated as a potential trigger for autoimmunity and disease flares in SLE** [N4-R2][N4-R5]. Another source adds that **stress can disrupt immunological function and has been identified as a triggering factor in up to 80% of patients prior to flare-ups** [N4-R3]. This indicates that stress is not merely a bystander but an active trigger in SLE.

In addition to psychological stress, the evidence set also points to **chronic stress** as relevant. The link between post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and SLE notes that **among those genetically predisposed to SLE, systemic inflammation that accompanies chronic stress may fan the flames of smoldering SLE by priming immune responses** [N4-R4]. This expands the concept of stress from momentary events to ongoing physiological and psychological burden.

Metabolic factors are also implicated. The broader SLE literature in the evidence set notes that **higher intake of free sugars is linked to greater disease activity and complications** [N3-R2], and that **nutritional status and unhealthy dietary habits may have an influence on SLE course and activity** [N3-R5]. This suggests that **dietary patterns and metabolic load can act as triggers or aggravating factors**.

### How stress and metabolic perturbations can dysregulate immunity

The mechanistic evidence explains how these stressors dysregulate immunity:

- **Stress-induced immunological disruption**: The stress evidence states that stress can **disrupt immunological function** and is a potential trigger for autoimmunity and disease flares [N4-R2][N4-R5]. It also notes that stress may **prime immune responses**, especially in the context of chronic stress and PTSD [N4-R4].
- **Metabolic stress and immune activation**: The calorie restriction review notes that CR can have immunomodulatory effects on innate and adaptive immune components, and that these effects operate through both cell-intrinsic and extrinsic pathways [N2-F3]. In SLE, calorie restriction and fast-mimicking diet are specifically mentioned as interventions used to investigate metabolic pathways and immune function [N2-R1]. This implies that metabolic perturbations can alter immune activation and disease course.
- **Oxidative stress and immune dysfunction**: The dietary and nutritional review notes that **oxidative stress serves as a trigger for autoimmunity, causing aberrant apoptotic processes, immune system dysfunction, and autoantibody production** [N7-R3]. This directly links metabolic and oxidative stress to SLE pathogenesis.

### How these mechanisms may interact with dietary restriction or fasting

The interaction between dietary/metabolic stress and fasting is important because fasting can itself be a form of metabolic perturbation. The evidence suggests that:

- **Short-term fasting can lower inflammatory factors and promote immune tolerance** in some contexts [N6-R1][N6-R2], but this does not mean fasting is universally safe in SLE.
- **Intermittent fasting can increase B-cell activation, autoantibody production, and autoantibody immune complex formation** in MRL/lpr mice, which is relevant to SLE [N1-F1]. This suggests that fasting can worsen autoimmunity in some settings.
- **Calorie restriction and fast-mimicking diet** are explicitly used as dietary interventions to study links between metabolic pathways and immune function [N2-R1]. This supports the idea that dietary restriction can alter immune and metabolic pathways in ways that may either mitigate or exacerbate disease.

- Avoid over-interpreting observational studies as proof of benefit or harm.

## Summary

The evidence for whether intermittent fasting influences flares in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is **inconclusive and inconsistent**. The broader mechanistic and clinical literature also shows that **fasting can have complex and opposing effects on the immune system**, and that **dietary/metabolic stress can worsen SLE through stress, oxidative stress, and inflammatory pathways** [N9][N10].

In short: **intermittent fasting is not established as a safe or universally beneficial intervention for SLE patients**, and clinicians should interpret the evidence cautiously.

---

## Key findings

### 1) Direct human evidence on fasting and SLE flares

The direct evidence from human studies is limited and mostly observational:

- The only directly relevant human study is a **retrospective cohort study of 100 SLE patients during Ramadan**, which assessed the impact of intermittent fasting on disease activity in patients with quiescent SLE [N1-F2].
- The study found **no significant difference in clinical activity before and after fasting**, except for **non-adherent patients** [N1-F2].
- The study therefore does **not support a clear causal link between intermittent fasting and flares** [N1-F2].
- There is also a pilot study on SLE flares, but it is not a fasting study and therefore not directly relevant to the question [N1-R2].

### 2) Mechanistic evidence on fasting and autoimmunity

The mechanistic evidence suggests that fasting can have **complex and sometimes opposing effects** on immunity:

- **Short-term fasting** can **lower inflammatory factors and promote immune tolerance** in some contexts [N6-R1][N6-R2].
- **Intermittent fasting can increase B-cell activation, autoantibody production, and autoantibody immune complex formation** in MRL/lpr mice, which is highly relevant to SLE [N1-F1].
- **Calorie restriction and fast-mimicking diet** are explicitly used as dietary interventions to investigate links between metabolic pathways and immune function [N2-R1].
- **Metabolic stress, oxidative stress, and inflammatory pathways** are implicated in immune dysregulation and autoimmunity [N2-F3][N7-R3].
- **Short-term fasting** and **prolonged calorie restriction** differ in their effects: short-term fasting may have tolerogenic effects, while prolonged calorie restriction can have broader physiological effects and potential harms [N2-F3].

### 3) Evidence on SLE flare triggers and dietary/metabolic stress

The literature on SLE flares also shows that **stress is a well-established trigger**:

- **Acute and chronic stress, particularly trauma-induced stress, has been linked to increased disease activity and flare-ups** [N4-R1].
- **Stress can disrupt immunological function** and is a potential trigger for autoimmunity and disease flares [N4-R2][N4-R5].
- **Stress can be a triggering factor in up to 80% of patients prior to flare-ups** [N4-R3].
- **Chronic stress and post-traumatic stress** may exacerbate smoldering SLE by priming immune responses [N4-R4].
- **Metabolic and oxidative stress** can also worsen SLE, with evidence linking free sugars, poor nutrition, and oxidative stress to disease activity and complications [N3-R2][N3-R5][N7-R3].

In this context, dietary restriction or fasting can be viewed as a **metabolic stressor**, and the effect depends on the type, duration, and metabolic environment of the restriction [N2-R1][N2-F3][N6-R1][N6-R2].

---

## Caveats

### 1) Study design limitations

The strongest human evidence is **observational or retrospective**, which means it is subject to important limitations:

- **Small sample size and non-randomization**: The Ramadan study included only 100 patients, which is modest for SLE [N1-F2].
- **Heterogeneity in patient populations and fasting regimen**: The study involved patients in remission or mild activity before fasting, and the fasting regimen was not fully described [N1-F2].
- **Dependence on treatment adherence**: The study relied on adherence as a proxy and found worse outcomes in **non-adherent patients**, indicating strong confounding [N1-F2].
- **Limited flare-specific outcome data**: The study reported **no significant difference in clinical activity**, but did not provide explicit flare rates or detailed biomarker changes [N1-F2].

### 2) Conflicting results

The evidence is **conflicting and mostly observational**, so clinicians should not overinterpret it as proof of benefit or harm:

- One human study found **no significant difference in clinical activity** after Ramadan fasting [N1-F2].
- Preclinical evidence suggests that **intermittent fasting can worsen lupus nephritis in mice** [N1-F1].
- Other mechanistic evidence suggests that short-term fasting can have **tolerogenic or anti-inflammatory effects** [N6-R1][N6-R2].
- The broader nutrition literature suggests that **diet and metabolic factors can influence SLE activity**, but does not support intermittent fasting as a specific recommendation [N3-R2][N3-R5].

### 3) Context-dependent effects

The evidence supports a **context-dependent interpretation**:

- **Short-term fasting** may have different effects from **prolonged calorie restriction** [N2-F3].
- **Short-term fasting** can lower inflammatory factors and promote immune tolerance in some contexts [N6-R1][N6-R2].
- **Intermittent fasting** can increase B-cell activation and autoantibody production in lupus [N1-F1].
- **Stress and metabolic perturbations** can dysregulate immunity and worsen SLE [N4-R1][N4-R4][N7-R3].

---

## Practical advice for rheumatologists

### 1) Which patient groups may be more sensitive to fasting-related flares?

Several patient groups may be more sensitive to fasting-related flares:

- **Patients with active or recently flared disease**: Stress and metabolic stress can worsen SLE, so fasting may be especially risky in active disease [N4-R1][N4-R4][N7-R3].
- **Patients with poor treatment adherence**: The Ramadan study found worse outcomes in **non-adherent patients**, indicating strong confounding [N1-F2].

- **Patients with a history of stress or trauma**: Stress is a well-established trigger for SLE flares, so patients with a history of stress or trauma may be more sensitive [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R4].
- **Patients taking immunosuppressive medications or biologics**: Although not directly addressed in the evidence, the broader context is that dietary interventions may interact with immune therapy [N1-F1][N2-F3].

### 2) How to interpret conflicting study results in clinical practice

Because the evidence is **weak, observational, and heterogeneous**, clinicians should:

- Treat the evidence as **low-grade and inconclusive** rather than definitive [N1-F2].
- Avoid over-interpreting observational studies as proof of benefit or harm.
- Be especially cautious when patients have **active disease, poor adherence, or other metabolic vulnerabilities**.
- Use **individualized clinical judgment** and discuss the risks and benefits with the patient.

### 3) Safer, evidence-based dietary recommendations for SLE patients

The evidence supports the following safer, evidence-based dietary recommendations:

- **Maintain a healthy weight** [N5-F4].
- **Follow a low-saturated-fat, low-cholesterol diet** [N5-F4].
- **Include omega-3 fatty acids, antioxidants, and adequate vitamin D status** [N5-F4].

- **Avoid excessive free sugar intake**, since higher free sugar intake is linked to greater disease activity and complications [N3-R2].

**Intermittent fasting is not established as a safe or universally beneficial intervention for SLE patients** [N1-F2]. The available evidence is **inconclusive, mostly observational, and context-dependent** [N1-F2][N2-F3][N6-R1][N6-R2]. - **In other contexts, short-term fasting may have anti-inflammatory effects**, but this is not evidence enough to recommend fasting broadly [N6-R1][N6-R2].

- **Limited flare-specific outcome data**: The study reported **no significant difference in clinical activity** before and after fasting, but the abstract does not provide explicit flare rates or detailed biomarker changes [N1-F2]. This means the evidence is **weak on direct flare outcomes**.

The only directly reported outcomes in the human evidence are:

- **No significant change in clinical activity** in the Ramadan cohort [N1-F2].
- **Non-adherent patients had worse outcomes**, suggesting that **treatment adherence is a critical confounder** [N1-F2].

Based on the provided evidence, the strongest human studies do **not** support a clear, direct link between intermittent fasting and SLE flares. The only human study directly relevant to the question is a **retrospective Ramadan cohort study** with **no significant difference in clinical activity**, but with important limitations such as small sample size, heterogeneity, and confounding by treatment adherence [N1-F2]. ## Clinical implications and practical guidance for rheumatologists

The available evidence suggests that **intermittent fasting is not yet established as a safe or universally beneficial intervention for SLE patients**, and the data are inconsistent enough that clinicians should treat it with caution. The strongest human evidence is a **retrospective cohort study of 100 SLE patients during Ramadan**, which found **no significant difference in clinical activity before and after fasting**, but also noted that **non-adherent patients had worse outcomes** and that the impact of intermittent fasting on autoimmune conditions such as SLE remains **poorly understood and ambiguous** [N1-F2]. This means that the literature is **not sufficient to support broad clinical recommendations**, and **conflicting results should be interpreted carefully**.

### Which patient groups may be more sensitive to fasting-related flares

Several patient groups appear to be **more sensitive to metabolic and immune stressors**, and therefore potentially more sensitive to fasting-related flares:

1. **Patients with active or recently flared disease**: The upstream evidence on flare triggers emphasizes that **stress, chronic stress, and metabolic/oxidative stress can worsen SLE** [N4-R1][N4-R4][N7-R3]. If fasting introduces metabolic perturbations or disrupts immune homeostasis, patients with active disease may be especially vulnerable to flare.
2. **Patients with poor treatment adherence**: The Ramadan study explicitly found that **non-adherent patients had worse outcomes**, suggesting that **non-adherence is a major confounder** [N1-F2]. In clinical practice, this implies that fasting should not be encouraged in patients whose disease is poorly controlled or whose treatment adherence is unstable.
3. **Patients with comorbidities that affect metabolism or immune regulation**: The evidence set notes that **higher intake of free sugars is linked to greater disease activity and complications**, and that **nutritional status and unhealthy dietary habits may influence SLE course and activity** [N3-R2][N3-R5]. Patients with diabetes, malnutrition, or other metabolic disorders may be more vulnerable to fasting-related metabolic stress.
4. **Patients with a history of stress or trauma**: The evidence on SLE flare triggers notes that **acute and chronic stress, particularly trauma-induced stress, has been linked to increased disease activity and flare-ups** [N4-R1], and that **stress can disrupt immunological function** and be a triggering factor in up to **80% of patients prior to flare-ups** [N4-R3]. Patients with a history of stress or trauma may be more sensitive to fasting-related immune perturbations.
5. **Patients taking immunosuppressive medications or biologics**: Although the evidence does not directly address medication interactions, the broader context is that **SLE management depends on immunosuppressive drugs**, and any dietary intervention that alters immune activation or autoantibody production could theoretically interact with therapy [N1-F1][N2-F3].

### How to interpret conflicting study results in clinical practice

The conflicting results should be interpreted with caution because the current evidence base is **weak and heterogeneous**:

- The human evidence is **mainly observational or retrospective**, so it cannot prove causality [N1-F2]. The only directly relevant human study is a **retrospective Ramadan cohort study**, which is limited by small sample size, heterogeneity, and confounding by treatment adherence [N1-F2].
- The mechanistic evidence is **preclinical and context-dependent**: in mice, **intermittent fasting can worsen lupus nephritis by increasing B-cell activation, autoantibody production, and autoantibody immune complex formation**, while in some settings, short-term fasting can **lower inflammatory factors and promote immune tolerance** [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2].
- The broader nutrition literature suggests that **diet and metabolic factors can influence SLE activity**, but it does not support a specific recommendation for intermittent fasting [N3-R2][N3-R5].
- The evidence on calorie restriction and IF also shows that **short-term fasting may have different effects from prolonged calorie restriction**, and that **prolonged CR may have harmful effects** such as excessive weight loss and infection susceptibility [N2-F3].

In practice, clinicians should therefore:

- Treat the evidence as **low-grade and inconclusive** rather than definitive.
- Avoid over-interpreting observational studies as proof of benefit or harm.
- Be especially cautious when patients have **active disease, poor adherence, or other metabolic vulnerabilities**.
- Use **individualized clinical judgment** and discuss the risks and benefits with the patient.

### Dietary recommendations that are safer and evidence-based for SLE patients

The evidence-based recommendations for SLE patients are much clearer than the evidence for intermittent fasting:

1. **Maintain a healthy weight** [N5-F4].
2. **Follow a low-saturated-fat, low-cholesterol diet** [N5-F4].
3. **Include omega-3 fatty acids, antioxidants, and adequate vitamin D status** [N5-F4].
4. **Eat a varied, balanced diet** [N5-R2].
5. **Avoid excessive free sugar intake**, since higher free sugar intake is linked to greater disease activity and complications [N3-R2].
6. **Avoid dietary practices that are not supported by evidence**, such as **fasting and plant-based diets in some contexts** [N5-R5].

# Integrated final answer for the rheumatologist

## Summary

The evidence for whether intermittent fasting influences flares in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is **inconclusive and inconsistent**. The strongest human study directly relevant to the question is a **retrospective cohort study of 100 SLE patients during Ramadan**, which found **no significant difference in clinical activity before and after fasting**, but noted that **non-adherent patients had worse outcomes** and that the impact of intermittent fasting on SLE remains **poorly understood and ambiguous** [N1-F2]. The broader mechanistic and clinical literature also shows that **fasting can have complex and opposing effects on the immune system**, and that **dietary/metabolic stress can worsen SLE through stress, oxidative stress, and inflammatory pathways** [N9][N10].

In short: **intermittent fasting is not established as a safe or universally beneficial intervention for SLE patients**, and clinicians should interpret the evidence cautiously.

---

## Key findings

### 1) Direct human evidence on fasting and SLE flares

The direct evidence from human studies is limited and mostly observational:

- The only directly relevant human study is a **retrospective cohort study of 100 SLE patients during Ramadan**, which assessed the impact of intermittent fasting on disease activity in patients with quiescent SLE [N1-F2].
- The study found **no significant difference in clinical activity before and after fasting**, except for **non-adherent patients** [N1-F2].
- The study therefore does **not support a clear causal link between intermittent fasting and flares** [N1-F2].
- There is also a pilot study on SLE flares, but it is not a fasting study and therefore not directly relevant to the question [N1-R2].

### 2) Mechanistic evidence on fasting and autoimmunity

The mechanistic evidence suggests that fasting can have **complex and sometimes opposing effects** on immunity:

- **Short-term fasting** can **lower inflammatory factors and promote immune tolerance** in some contexts [N6-R1][N6-R2].
- **Intermittent fasting can increase B-cell activation, autoantibody production, and autoantibody immune complex formation** in MRL/lpr mice, which is highly relevant to SLE [N1-F1].
- **Calorie restriction and fast-mimicking diet** are explicitly used as dietary interventions to investigate links between metabolic pathways and immune function [N2-R1].
- **Metabolic stress, oxidative stress, and inflammatory pathways** are implicated in immune dysregulation and autoimmunity [N2-F3][N7-R3].
- **Short-term fasting** and **prolonged calorie restriction** differ in their effects: short-term fasting may have tolerogenic effects, while prolonged calorie restriction can have broader physiological effects and potential harms [N2-F3].

### 3) Evidence on SLE flare triggers and dietary/metabolic stress

The literature on SLE flares also shows that **stress is a well-established trigger**:

- **Acute and chronic stress, particularly trauma-induced stress, has been linked to increased disease activity and flare-ups** [N4-R1].
- **Stress can disrupt immunological function** and is a potential trigger for autoimmunity and disease flares [N4-R2][N4-R5].
- **Stress can be a triggering factor in up to 80% of patients prior to flare-ups** [N4-R3].
- **Chronic stress and post-traumatic stress** may exacerbate smoldering SLE by priming immune responses [N4-R4].
- **Metabolic and oxidative stress** can also worsen SLE, with evidence linking free sugars, poor nutrition, and oxidative stress to disease activity and complications [N3-R2][N3-R5][N7-R3].

In this context, dietary restriction or fasting can be viewed as a **metabolic stressor**, and the effect depends on the type, duration, and metabolic environment of the restriction [N2-R1][N2-F3][N6-R1][N6-R2].

---

## Caveats

### 1) Study design limitations

The strongest human evidence is **observational or retrospective**, which means it is subject to important limitations:

- **Small sample size and non-randomization**: The Ramadan study included only 100 patients, which is modest for SLE [N1-F2].
- **Heterogeneity in patient populations and fasting regimen**: The study involved patients in remission or mild activity before fasting, and the fasting regimen was not fully described [N1-F2].
- **Dependence on treatment adherence**: The study relied on adherence as a proxy and found worse outcomes in **non-adherent patients**, indicating strong confounding [N1-F2].
- **Limited flare-specific outcome data**: The study reported **no significant difference in clinical activity**, but did not provide explicit flare rates or detailed biomarker changes [N1-F2].

### 2) Conflicting results

The evidence is **conflicting and mostly observational**, so clinicians should not overinterpret it as proof of benefit or harm:

- One human study found **no significant difference in clinical activity** after Ramadan fasting [N1-F2].
- Preclinical evidence suggests that **intermittent fasting can worsen lupus nephritis in mice** [N1-F1].
- Other mechanistic evidence suggests that short-term fasting can have **tolerogenic or anti-inflammatory effects** [N6-R1][N6-R2].
- The broader nutrition literature suggests that **diet and metabolic factors can influence SLE activity**, but does not support intermittent fasting as a specific recommendation [N3-R2][N3-R5].

### 3) Context-dependent effects

## Strongest human studies on fasting and SLE flares

The direct human evidence for intermittent fasting (IF) and SLE flares is limited and currently inconclusive. The most relevant human study in the evidence set is a **retrospective cohort study of 100 SLE patients in Egypt during Ramadan**, which aimed to assess the impact of intermittent fasting on disease activity in patients with quiescent SLE [N1-F2]. This study found **no significant difference in clinical activity before and after fasting**, except for a notable exception in **non-adherent patients to treatment** [N1-F2]. This is an important finding, but it is **not a randomized controlled trial (RCT)** and therefore cannot definitively prove causality.

A second relevant human study is the **Springer article on the impact of intermittent fasting on systemic lupus erythematosus disease activity**, which is likely the same retrospective cohort study [N1-F2]. The abstract and excerpt suggest that the study assessed **disease activity through SLEDAI score, laboratory work, and treatment adherence**, with the main conclusion being that Ramadan fasting may be **safe and beneficial** for patients in milder stages of the disease who strictly adhere to treatment [N1-F2]. However, the excerpt also notes that the precise impact of intermittent fasting on autoimmune conditions such as SLE remains **poorly understood and ambiguous** [N1-F2].

The evidence set also includes a **pilot study on SLE flares**, described as assessing changes in quality of life at the end of a 16-week Mymee program in patients with moderate to severe SLE [N1-R2]. This is not a fasting study, so it does not directly address the question of whether fasting influences flares.

### Study design limitations

The strongest human evidence is therefore **observational or retrospective**, which means it is subject to important limitations:

- **Small sample size and non-randomization**: The Ramadan study included 100 SLE patients, which is modest for a condition as variable as SLE, especially when outcomes depend on disease activity scores and treatment adherence [N1-F2]. The study was also retrospective and non-randomized, so **confounding by treatment adherence, disease activity baseline, and other unmeasured variables is likely** [N1-F2].
- **Heterogeneity in patient populations and fasting regimen**: The Ramadan study involved patients in remission or mild activity before fasting, and the fasting regimen was not described in detail beyond the timing of Ramadan [N1-F2]. This makes it difficult to generalize to other IF regimens or to patients with more active disease.
- **Dependence on self-reported or proxy-reported adherence**: The study relied on treatment adherence as a proxy, which can be imperfect and is especially vulnerable to bias in retrospective settings [N1-F2].
- **Limited flare-specific outcome data**: The study reported **no significant difference in clinical activity** before and after fasting, but the abstract does not provide explicit flare rates or detailed biomarker changes [N1-F2]. This means the evidence is **weak on direct flare outcomes**.

### Reported outcomes

The only directly reported outcomes in the human evidence are:

- **No significant change in clinical activity** in the Ramadan cohort [N1-F2].
- **Non-adherent patients had worse outcomes**, suggesting that **treatment adherence is a critical confounder** [N1-F2].
- **SLEDAI score assessment** and other laboratory measures were used to evaluate disease activity, but the excerpt does not provide specific values or a clear comparison of flare rates [N1-F2].

In addition, the broader context from the nutrition and diet literature is that **weight loss and low-calorie diets can be safe and well-tolerated in SLE**, but this is not the same as evidence for intermittent fasting [N3-R1]. Another review notes that **higher intake of free sugars is linked to greater disease activity and complications**, and that **not all obese patients share the same response** to weight loss [N3-R2]. This highlights that **diet-related changes in body composition and metabolism can affect disease activity**, but it does not prove that intermittent fasting itself is protective or harmful.

### Overall conclusion

Based on the provided evidence, the strongest human studies do **not** support a clear, direct link between intermittent fasting and SLE flares. The only human study directly relevant to the question is a **retrospective Ramadan cohort study** with **no significant difference in clinical activity**, but with important limitations such as small sample size, heterogeneity, and confounding by treatment adherence [N1-F2]. The broader literature on nutrition and SLE suggests that **diet and metabolic factors can influence disease activity**, but the evidence for intermittent fasting is thin and inconsistent [N3-R1][N3-R2].

## Biological mechanisms linking fasting to immune activation or tolerance

The mechanistic evidence suggests that fasting can have **complex and sometimes opposing effects on the immune system**, with important differences between **short-term fasting** and **prolonged calorie restriction**.

### Effects on cytokines, B cells, T cells, and autoantibodies

A key review on calorie restriction and its mimetics states that CR can have **immunomodulatory effects on both innate and adaptive immune components**, including T and B lymphocytes, and that the mechanisms are complex and context-dependent [N2-F3]. It also notes that CR has been shown to improve symptoms and pathological features of some autoimmune diseases, but the evidence is strongest in preclinical models rather than human studies [N2-F3].

The mechanistic review on intermittent fasting and immunity adds that IF can **benefit health subjects by strengthening circadian rhythms, migrating immune cells, lowering inflammatory factors, and enriching microbials** [N6-R1]. It also suggests that **B and T lymphocytes are among the immune cell types most affected by IF**, with evidence of changes in neutrophils and lymphocyte populations [N6-R2]. Another source notes that fasting in mice significantly reduced lymphocytes in PPs by approximately 50%, with migration of naive B cells to the bone marrow and other changes in immune-cell trafficking [N6-R4].

At the autoantibody level, the mechanistic evidence is especially relevant to SLE. A review on B cell metabolism in autoimmune diseases explains that **self-tolerance failure leads to auto-reactive B cells producing autoantibodies and pro-inflammatory cytokines**, which drives autoimmune disease [N6-R3]. Another source states that B cells are central to the pathogenesis of multiple autoimmune diseases through antigen presentation, cytokine secretion, and autoantibody production [N6-R5]. This is directly relevant because SLE is characterized by **autoantibody production, particularly anti-dsDNA antibodies**, and the evidence from the MRL/lpr mouse study shows that IF can increase **anti-dsDNA antibody levels, immune complex deposition, and autoantibody-mediated tissue damage** [N1-F1].

### Metabolic stress, oxidative stress, or inflammatory pathways

The mechanistic evidence supports several pathways that may link fasting to immune dysregulation:

- **Metabolic stress**: CR and IF induce changes in intracellular metabolism and signaling, which can influence immune cell function [N2-F3]. In SLE, calorie restriction and fast-mimicking diet are specifically highlighted as dietary interventions used to investigate links between metabolic pathways and immune function [N2-R1].
- **Oxidative stress**: The dietary and nutritional evidence in SLE includes a scoping review that links dietary factors to oxidative stress, aberrant apoptosis, immune dysfunction, and autoimmunity [N7-R3]. This supports the idea that metabolic and oxidative stress can worsen autoimmune disease.
- **Inflammatory pathways**: The review on calorie restriction notes that CR can reduce inflammatory molecules and modulate immune responses through both cell-intrinsic and extrinsic pathways [N2-F3]. The MRL/lpr mouse study also found that IF increased **IFN-γ production** and worsened immune complex deposition and glomerular injury [N1-F1]. This suggests that IF can shift the inflammatory profile in a pro-autoimmune direction in some settings.

### Differences between short-term fasting and prolonged calorie restriction

The evidence set indicates that short-term fasting and prolonged calorie restriction may not be equivalent:

- **Short-term fasting**: The mechanistic review on intermittent fasting states that fasting can **lower inflammatory factors** and promote **immune tolerance** in some contexts [N6-R1]. It also notes that IF with a fasting-refeeding switch appears to promote immune tolerance [N6-R2]. This suggests that short-term fasting can have **protective or tolerogenic effects** in some immune settings.
- **Prolonged calorie restriction**: The CR review emphasizes that CR induces complex physiological changes that affect the immune system, including both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways, and that it is a powerful intervention with broad health benefits [N2-F3]. However, it also notes that **chronic CR may have harmful health effects**, such as excessive weight loss and increased susceptibility to infection [N2-F3]. This implies that prolonged calorie restriction can be beneficial but also carries risks that may differ from short-term fasting.

In the SLE context, the mouse study is especially informative because it shows that **IF can worsen lupus nephritis by increasing B-cell activation, autoantibody production, and autoantibody immune complex formation** [N1-F1]. This contrasts with some short-term fasting effects on immune tolerance, indicating that **the direction of effect depends on the model and the disease context**.

### Bottom line

The biological mechanisms suggest that fasting can both **lower inflammatory factors and promote immune tolerance in some contexts** [N6-R1][N6-R2], but the same evidence also shows that **short-term fasting can increase B-cell activation and autoantibody production in lupus** [N1-F1]. The mechanistic literature therefore supports a **context-dependent interpretation**: fasting may be beneficial in some immune settings, harmful in others, and likely influenced by the duration, intensity, and metabolic environment of the restriction.

## Mechanisms of flare triggers and how dietary/metabolic stress may worsen SLE

### Which stressors and metabolic factors are known to trigger SLE flares

The evidence shows that **stress is a well-established trigger for SLE flares**. The stress-related evidence set explicitly states that **acute and chronic stress, particularly trauma-induced stress, has been linked to increased disease activity and flare-ups in SLE** [N4-R1]. It also notes that **stress has been evaluated as a potential trigger for autoimmunity and disease flares in SLE** [N4-R2][N4-R5]. Another source adds that **stress can disrupt immunological function and has been identified as a triggering factor in up to 80% of patients prior to flare-ups** [N4-R3]. This indicates that stress is not merely a bystander but an active trigger in SLE.

In addition to psychological stress, the evidence set also points to **chronic stress** as relevant. The link between post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and SLE notes that **among those genetically predisposed to SLE, systemic inflammation that accompanies chronic stress may fan the flames of smoldering SLE by priming immune responses** [N4-R4]. This expands the concept of stress from momentary events to ongoing physiological and psychological burden.

Metabolic factors are also implicated. The broader SLE literature in the evidence set notes that **higher intake of free sugars is linked to greater disease activity and complications** [N3-R2], and that **nutritional status and unhealthy dietary habits may have an influence on SLE course and activity** [N3-R5]. This suggests that **dietary patterns and metabolic load can act as triggers or aggravating factors**.

### How stress and metabolic perturbations can dysregulate immunity

The mechanistic evidence explains how these stressors dysregulate immunity:

- **Stress-induced immunological disruption**: The stress evidence states that stress can **disrupt immunological function** and is a potential trigger for autoimmunity and disease flares [N4-R2][N4-R5]. It also notes that stress may **prime immune responses**, especially in the context of chronic stress and PTSD [N4-R4].
- **Metabolic stress and immune activation**: The calorie restriction review notes that CR can have immunomodulatory effects on innate and adaptive immune components, and that these effects operate through both cell-intrinsic and extrinsic pathways [N2-F3]. In SLE, calorie restriction and fast-mimicking diet are specifically mentioned as interventions used to investigate metabolic pathways and immune function [N2-R1]. This implies that metabolic perturbations can alter immune activation and disease course.
- **Oxidative stress and immune dysfunction**: The dietary and nutritional review notes that **oxidative stress serves as a trigger for autoimmunity, causing aberrant apoptotic processes, immune system dysfunction, and autoantibody production** [N7-R3]. This directly links metabolic and oxidative stress to SLE pathogenesis.

### How these mechanisms may interact with dietary restriction or fasting

The interaction between dietary/metabolic stress and fasting is important because fasting can itself be a form of metabolic perturbation. The evidence suggests that:

- **Short-term fasting can lower inflammatory factors and promote immune tolerance** in some contexts [N6-R1][N6-R2], but this does not mean fasting is universally safe in SLE.
- **Intermittent fasting can increase B-cell activation, autoantibody production, and autoantibody immune complex formation** in MRL/lpr mice, which is relevant to SLE [N1-F1]. This suggests that fasting can worsen autoimmunity in some settings.
- **Calorie restriction and fast-mimicking diet** are explicitly used as dietary interventions to study links between metabolic pathways and immune function [N2-R1]. This supports the idea that dietary restriction can alter immune and metabolic pathways in ways that may either mitigate or exacerbate disease.
- **Dietary and nutritional factors** can influence SLE course and activity, including oxidative stress and immune dysfunction [N3-R5][N7-R3]. Therefore, fasting and other dietary patterns are not neutral; they can perturb the same pathways that are already dysregulated in SLE.

### Bottom line

The strongest mechanistic conclusion is that **SLE flares are triggered by stress, chronic stress, and metabolic/oxidative stress**, and that these same stressors and perturbations can dysregulate immunity through inflammatory, oxidative, and metabolic pathways [N4-R1][N4-R4][N3-R5][N7-R3]. In this context, **dietary restriction or fasting can act as a metabolic stressor**, and the evidence suggests that the effect depends on the type, duration, and metabolic environment of the restriction [N2-R1][N2-F3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N1-F1]. This means that dietary interventions should be viewed as potentially **dual-edged**, with the potential to either reduce or increase disease activity depending on the patient and the intervention.

## Clinical implications and practical guidance for rheumatologists

The available evidence suggests that **intermittent fasting is not yet established as a safe or universally beneficial intervention for SLE patients**, and the data are inconsistent enough that clinicians should treat it with caution. The strongest human evidence is a **retrospective cohort study of 100 SLE patients during Ramadan**, which found **no significant difference in clinical activity before and after fasting**, but also noted that **non-adherent patients had worse outcomes** and that the impact of intermittent fasting on autoimmune conditions such as SLE remains **poorly understood and ambiguous** [N1-F2]. This means that the literature is **not sufficient to support broad clinical recommendations**, and **conflicting results should be interpreted carefully**.

### Which patient groups may be more sensitive to fasting-related flares

Several patient groups appear to be **more sensitive to metabolic and immune stressors**, and therefore potentially more sensitive to fasting-related flares:

1. **Patients with active or recently flared disease**: The upstream evidence on flare triggers emphasizes that **stress, chronic stress, and metabolic/oxidative stress can worsen SLE** [N4-R1][N4-R4][N7-R3]. If fasting introduces metabolic perturbations or disrupts immune homeostasis, patients with active disease may be especially vulnerable to flare.
2. **Patients with poor treatment adherence**: The Ramadan study explicitly found that **non-adherent patients had worse outcomes**, suggesting that **non-adherence is a major confounder** [N1-F2]. In clinical practice, this implies that fasting should not be encouraged in patients whose disease is poorly controlled or whose treatment adherence is unstable.
3. **Patients with comorbidities that affect metabolism or immune regulation**: The evidence set notes that **higher intake of free sugars is linked to greater disease activity and complications**, and that **nutritional status and unhealthy dietary habits may influence SLE course and activity** [N3-R2][N3-R5]. Patients with diabetes, malnutrition, or other metabolic disorders may be more vulnerable to fasting-related metabolic stress.
4. **Patients with a history of stress or trauma**: The evidence on SLE flare triggers notes that **acute and chronic stress, particularly trauma-induced stress, has been linked to increased disease activity and flare-ups** [N4-R1], and that **stress can disrupt immunological function** and be a triggering factor in up to **80% of patients prior to flare-ups** [N4-R3]. Patients with a history of stress or trauma may be more sensitive to fasting-related immune perturbations.
5. **Patients taking immunosuppressive medications or biologics**: Although the evidence does not directly address medication interactions, the broader context is that **SLE management depends on immunosuppressive drugs**, and any dietary intervention that alters immune activation or autoantibody production could theoretically interact with therapy [N1-F1][N2-F3].

### How to interpret conflicting study results in clinical practice

The conflicting results should be interpreted with caution because the current evidence base is **weak and heterogeneous**:

- The human evidence is **mainly observational or retrospective**, so it cannot prove causality [N1-F2]. The only directly relevant human study is a **retrospective Ramadan cohort study**, which is limited by small sample size, heterogeneity, and confounding by treatment adherence [N1-F2].
- The mechanistic evidence is **preclinical and context-dependent**: in mice, **intermittent fasting can worsen lupus nephritis by increasing B-cell activation, autoantibody production, and autoantibody immune complex formation**, while in some settings, short-term fasting can **lower inflammatory factors and promote immune tolerance** [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2].
- The broader nutrition literature suggests that **diet and metabolic factors can influence SLE activity**, but it does not support a specific recommendation for intermittent fasting [N3-R2][N3-R5].
- The evidence on calorie restriction and IF also shows that **short-term fasting may have different effects from prolonged calorie restriction**, and that **prolonged CR may have harmful effects** such as excessive weight loss and infection susceptibility [N2-F3].

In practice, clinicians should therefore:

- Treat the evidence as **low-grade and inconclusive** rather than definitive.
- Avoid over-interpreting observational studies as proof of benefit or harm.
- Be especially cautious when patients have **active disease, poor adherence, or other metabolic vulnerabilities**.
- Use **individualized clinical judgment** and discuss the risks and benefits with the patient.

### Dietary recommendations that are safer and evidence-based for SLE patients

The evidence-based recommendations for SLE patients are much clearer than the evidence for intermittent fasting:

1. **Maintain a healthy weight** [N5-F4].
2. **Follow a low-saturated-fat, low-cholesterol diet** [N5-F4].
3. **Include omega-3 fatty acids, antioxidants, and adequate vitamin D status** [N5-F4].
4. **Eat a varied, balanced diet** [N5-R2].
5. **Avoid excessive free sugar intake**, since higher free sugar intake is linked to greater disease activity and complications [N3-R2].
6. **Avoid dietary practices that are not supported by evidence**, such as **fasting and plant-based diets in some contexts** [N5-R5].
7. **Ensure adequate nutrition** to support immune and metabolic health, especially in patients with renal involvement or malnutrition [N3-R5][N5-F4].

The clinical guideline excerpt emphasizes that **dietary changes, physical activity, smoking cessation, and avoidance of harmful exposures** should be part of SLE management, but it also states that **fasting and plant-based diets should not be proposed to patients** in some guidelines [N5-F4][N5-R5]. This is an important practical signal for rheumatologists.

### Bottom line

In practical terms, the evidence supports the following conclusions:

- **Intermittent fasting is not established as safe or beneficial for SLE patients** [N1-F2].
- **The evidence is conflicting and mostly observational**, so **clinical recommendations should be cautious and individualized** [N1-F2][N2-F3].
- **Patients with active disease, poor adherence, stress history, or metabolic vulnerabilities are likely more sensitive** to fasting-related flares [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R4][N1-F1].
- **Safer, evidence-based dietary advice** is to focus on **healthy weight, balanced nutrition, omega-3s, antioxidants, vitamin D, and avoidance of excessive sugar** [N5-F4][N3-R2][N3-R5].
- **Clinicians should avoid proposing fasting as a routine intervention** unless the evidence is stronger and the patient’s disease status is well-controlled.

In short: **intermittent fasting is not a proven therapeutic option for SLE, and the safest practical approach is to follow standard evidence-based nutrition guidelines** [N5-F4][N3-R2].

The broader mechanistic and clinical literature also shows that **fasting can have complex and opposing effects on the immune system**, and that **dietary/metabolic stress can worsen SLE through stress, oxidative stress, and inflammatory pathways** [N9][N10].

---

### 1) Direct human evidence on fasting and SLE flares

The direct evidence from human studies is limited and mostly observational:

- The only directly relevant human study is a **retrospective cohort study of 100 SLE patients during Ramadan**, which assessed the impact of intermittent fasting on disease activity in patients with quiescent SLE [N1-F2].
- The study found **no significant difference in clinical activity before and after fasting**, except for **non-adherent patients** [N1-F2].
- The study therefore does **not support a clear causal link between intermittent fasting and flares** [N1-F2].
- There is also a pilot study on SLE flares, but it is not a fasting study and therefore not directly relevant to the question [N1-R2].

### 2) Mechanistic evidence on fasting and autoimmunity

The mechanistic evidence suggests that fasting can have **complex and sometimes opposing effects** on immunity:

- **Short-term fasting** can **lower inflammatory factors and promote immune tolerance** in some contexts [N6-R1][N6-R2].
- **Intermittent fasting can increase B-cell activation, autoantibody production, and autoantibody immune complex formation** in MRL/lpr mice, which is highly relevant to SLE [N1-F1].
- **Calorie restriction and fast-mimicking diet** are explicitly used as dietary interventions to investigate links between metabolic pathways and immune function [N2-R1].

- **Short-term fasting** and **prolonged calorie restriction** differ in their effects: short-term fasting may have tolerogenic effects, while prolonged calorie restriction can have broader physiological effects and potential harms [N2-F3].

The literature on SLE flares also shows that **stress is a well-established trigger**:

- **Acute and chronic stress, particularly trauma-induced stress, has been linked to increased disease activity and flare-ups** [N4-R1].

### 1) Study design limitations

The strongest human evidence is **observational or retrospective**, which means it is subject to important limitations:

- **Short-term fasting** may have different effects from **prolonged calorie restriction** [N2-F3].

Because the evidence is **weak, observational, and heterogeneous**, clinicians should:

- Treat the evidence as **low-grade and inconclusive** rather than definitive [N1-F2].
